title: The teaching is the refuge
hookLine: after the Buddha's death Ananda says the dhamma is their refuge

lines: RAJAGAHA, JUST AFTER THE BUDDHA'S DEATH.
cards: When a founder dies, one question comes fast: who's in charge now? Bands face it, and family businesses. The hundred and eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings is set just after the Buddha's death.

Ananda, his attendant, is in the city of Rajagaha. The kingdom is nervous; the city's walls are being strengthened against a rival king. And a powerful minister named Vassakara comes to ask Ananda exactly that question.

teach.h: NO ONE HAS ALL HIS QUALITIES
teach.b: It starts with a smaller question. Ananda visits a brahmin named Gopaka Moggallana at a building site. Is there any monk, Gopaka asks, who has every quality the Buddha had?
No, says Ananda. The Buddha found a path that wasn't known; his students only follow it.
Then Vassakara arrives and presses harder. Did the Buddha appoint a monk to be your refuge after him? No.
Did the community choose one? No. Then you have no refuge.
So what keeps you together? Ananda turns the question around. We are not without a refuge, he says.
The teaching is our refuge. Then he gets practical. There's a training code, recited together on the moon days.
Whoever has slipped says so, and the group handles it by the teaching, not by anyone's favor. No monk gives the orders; the teaching does. That doesn't mean nobody is respected.
Yes, Ananda says, they honor certain monks, but for what they live: virtue, learning, contentment, stillness and insight.
Respect follows the practice, not a title.
This fits what the Buddha said near the end of his life, in another discourse: be islands to yourselves, with the teaching as your refuge. Ananda isn't improvising; he's doing what he was told.
Monastic communities still gather to recite a shared code together. When the founder is gone, the refuge is what he left in their hands.

how: Theravada monastic communities recite the Patimokkha, the training code, together on the new-moon and full-moon observance days, and seniority and respect within the community rest on ordination and conduct rather than on a single appointed leader of the whole tradition.

o: a leader appointed to replace the Buddha
a shelter built for monks in the rains
having the teaching itself as your refuge

games.q: after the Buddha: tap the pairs.
p: asked: does any monk have all his qualities?
the minister who asked about a successor
recited together on the moon days

s: the Buddha named a monk to lead everyone after him
in MN 108, Ananda says he appointed no one, and the community chose no one either.
Ananda says the monks honor some of their number
for their virtue, learning, contentment, stillness and insight: respect follows practice.
Ananda says that without a leader they have no refuge
he says the opposite: we are not without a refuge; the teaching is our refuge.

games.q: you're Ananda. a powerful minister says: with no leader appointed, you have no refuge. what do you say?
o: we'll choose a new leader soon.
we have a refuge: the teaching.
games.why: Ananda says the community isn't without a refuge. the teaching is the refuge, and the shared training code keeps them in harmony.

practice: Let the breath arrive on its own, and bring to mind one teaching from this year that has stayed with you, a line, a simile, a story.
Don't think about who said it or who's in charge of it; let it sit in your chest like something you own. If you say the refuges, you might recall them quietly now; if not, just rest with the line.

wordCard.voice: Dhammappatisarana. Having the teaching as refuge: after the Buddha's death, with no appointed heir, Ananda tells a minister the community stands on the teaching itself.

orig.note: Pali dhammappatisarana: having the teaching as refuge. Ananda's word for the community after the Buddha.

carryVoice: Your line: respect follows the practice. The teaching you already have is the refuge. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta (be islands to yourselves, the dhamma as refuge)
